title: Federated learning: training without moving the data
summary: FedAvg worked through on three clients with real arithmetic, the rounds it buys, how label skew drifts it to the wrong answer, and what quorums, secure aggregation and differential privacy change.
outcomes: Explain why the data cannot be centralized and write the federated objective as a weighted sum of per-client losses
Compute a FedAvg round by hand: local updates on three clients and the average weighted by sample count
Explain the communication and computation tradeoff of more local epochs, and when extra local work makes things worse
Predict how a label-skewed split drifts FedAvg to a biased fixed point, and say what FedProx and SCAFFOLD change
Describe what a server does and does not see under secure aggregation, and read the privacy and utility cost of DP

lessons.title: The setting: data that is not allowed to leave the device

blocks.md:
You already know the centralized recipe: collect a dataset, compute the average loss over it, and walk the parameters downhill with gradient descent. Federated learning keeps that objective and throws away the collection step.

The motivating case is a phone keyboard. Everything you type is exactly the data that would improve next-word prediction, and it is exactly the data you would least like uploaded. Google's Gboard trained a next-word model this way on real phones: about 1.4 million parameters, 3000 rounds, data from 1.5 million users, with each round taking two to three minutes of wall-clock time. The same shape appears across organizations rather than devices: hospitals or banks that each hold records they are not permitted to pool.

Three obvious approaches fail, each for its own reason.

1. **Upload the raw data.** Often blocked by policy or law, and the raw logs are usually much bigger than the model you want to train.
2. **Train on one device alone.** A single phone holds a few hundred examples of one person's typing. That model overfits its owner and never sees the vocabulary of everyone else.
3. **Send a gradient every step.** Mathematically clean, and it is the baseline called FedSGD, but each step costs a network round trip to a phone on home wifi. Reaching 99 percent on a small image model this way took 626 rounds in the original experiments, where a smarter scheme took 18.

blocks.tex: f(w) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{n_k}{n} F_k(w), \qquad F_k(w) = \frac{1}{n_k} \sum_{i \in P_k} \ell(w; x_i, y_i)
blocks.caption: The federated objective. Client k holds the example set P_k of size n_k, and n is the total over all K clients. This is algebraically identical to the pooled average loss: only the bookkeeping is split up. Clients with more data pull harder.

blocks.md: The defining property is not cryptography. It is that **the data stays put and only parameters move**. In the standard description of the setting, a central orchestration server organizes the training but never sees raw data.

blocks.title: Three ways to use data that lives on phones

scenes.caption: Option 1: ship the raw examples to a datacenter and train normally. This is the approach that privacy policy, regulation and upload bandwidth all rule out.
Option 2: let each phone train only on itself. Phone A has 54 examples of one person's typing, so the model it learns is both tiny and personal to the point of useless for everyone else.
The federated round, step 1: the server selects some clients and broadcasts the current global model to each of them. The datacenter copy of the data never exists.
Step 2: each selected client runs several local epochs of ordinary SGD on its own examples, starting from the broadcast model. The examples never leave the box they are in.
Step 3: only parameters travel back, and the server averages them weighted by how many examples each client trained on. One round is done; now repeat a few thousand times.

blocks.md:
Two regimes get used in practice, and they differ in almost every systems dimension.

**Cross-device**: the clients are phones or IoT devices. The population runs up to $10^{10}$ clients, only a fraction are reachable at any moment with a strong day and night cycle, clients cannot be addressed individually, they are stateless (a client usually participates once and never again), and 5 percent or more of a round's clients are expected to fail or drop out mid-round.

**Cross-silo**: the clients are typically 2 to 100 organizations or geo-distributed datacenters. They are stateful, addressable, almost always available, and failures are rare. Communication may or may not be the bottleneck.

Typical orders of magnitude for a cross-device application: 50 to 5000 devices selected per round, $10^5$ to $10^7$ devices touched over the life of a model, 500 to 10000 rounds, and 1 to 10 days of wall-clock training.

blocks.prompt: You have 100 phones, each with 600 examples, and you can afford 100 network round trips total. Would you rather spend each round trip on one gradient step from every phone, or on each phone doing a few hundred local steps?
blocks.reveal: Local steps, by a wide margin, and this is the whole design. In the original MNIST experiments the one-gradient-per-round scheme (FedSGD) needed 626 rounds to hit 99 percent, while letting each client run 20 local epochs with batch size 10 needed 18 rounds for the same accuracy. You have no budget problem on the devices (they are idle and charging), and a severe budget problem on the network. Lesson 3 quantifies exactly when this trade stops working.

blocks.question: Eight hospitals want one shared model and no record may leave any hospital. What is the training objective?
options: Each hospital trains alone and the best of the eight models is shipped
The same pooled average loss as centralized training, written as a sum of per-hospital losses weighted by record count
The unweighted mean of the eight per-hospital losses, since each hospital is one client
A new objective that no centralized training run could express
blocks.explain: Federated learning changes who computes, not what is being minimized. The objective is the pooled average loss, which factors exactly into a sum over clients with weights n_k/n. The unweighted mean is a different objective: it would give a hospital with 200 records the same influence as one with 20000.

blocks.question: In cross-device federated learning, which expectation is realistic for a single round?
options: Every device in the population contributes once per round
The same few hundred devices are reused every round so they can carry state
A few hundred devices are chosen from the much larger set currently available, and some of them will not report back
Devices are addressed by identifier so the server can retry a specific one
blocks.explain: Availability is the constraint. Tens of thousands of devices may be checking in, the server picks a few hundred, clients are not individually addressable and are treated as stateless, and 5 percent or more of a round's participants are expected to drop out. Carrying per-client state across rounds is a cross-silo luxury.

lessons.title: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds

blocks.md:
FedAvg is four lines. The server keeps a model $w_t$. Each round it samples a fraction $C$ of the $K$ clients, sends them $w_t$, and each selected client runs $E$ epochs of plain SGD over its local data with minibatch size $B$ and learning rate $\eta$, then sends back the parameters it ended up with. The server replaces $w_t$ with a weighted average of those parameter vectors, weighting client k by how many examples it trained on.

That is it. No gradients are sent, no data is sent, and the only thing the algorithm knows about a client is its parameter vector and its sample count.

blocks.code:
# Algorithm 1 of McMahan et al. 2017, written as Python
def federated_averaging(K, C, E, B, eta, rounds):
    w = init_model()
    for t in range(rounds):
        m = max(int(C * K), 1)
        S = sample_clients(m)                   # server picks who trains
        results = []
        for k in S:                             # in parallel, on devices
            results.append((n[k], client_update(k, w, E, B, eta)))
        m_t = sum(n_k for n_k, _ in results)    # examples in THIS round
        w = sum((n_k / m_t) * w_k for n_k, w_k in results)
    return w

def client_update(k, w, E, B, eta):
    for epoch in range(E):
        for batch in split(local_data[k], B):
            w = w - eta * grad_loss(w, batch)
    return w                                    # parameters, not data
blocks.caption: B set to the whole local dataset means one full-batch step per epoch. The paper writes that case as B equal to infinity.

blocks.tex: w_{t+1} = \sum_{k \in S_t} \frac{n_k}{m_t} w_{t+1}^{k}, \qquad m_t = \sum_{k \in S_t} n_k
blocks.caption: The aggregation step. Note that the weights are normalized over the clients that actually reported in this round, not over all K clients; an erratum in the paper corrected an earlier version that divided by the full n.

blocks.md: Three knobs control the cost. $C$ is the fraction of clients per round, and the experiments settle on $C = 0.1$ as a good balance. $E$ is the number of local epochs and $B$ the local minibatch size; together they set how much work a client does before it is allowed to talk. The expected number of SGD updates a client performs per round is

blocks.caption: Local updates per client per round, and its expectation over a uniformly drawn client. With 600 examples per client, E equal to 20 and B equal to 10, one client does 1200 SGD steps between two network messages.

blocks.md:
Now real arithmetic. The toy problem is a one-parameter least squares fit: the model predicts $\hat{y} = w x$ and the loss on one point is $\frac{1}{2}(w x - y)^2$, half the squared error so the derivative carries no stray 2. There are 108 points of three kinds, and three clients.

- Client A holds 54 copies of $(x, y) = (1, 1)$
- Client B holds 36 copies of $(x, y) = (2, 4)$
- Client C holds 18 copies of $(x, y) = (3, 9)$

Each client's loss is a parabola in $w$, with its own minimum $\mu_k$ and its own curvature $a_k$. The script that produced every number below computes them as exact fractions: $\mu = 1, 2, 3$ and $a = 1, 4, 9$. The weights are $p_k = n_k/n = 1/2, 1/3, 1/6$, and the minimum of the pooled objective is $w^{*} = 2.3$ exactly.

blocks.caption: Local full-batch gradient step for this problem, with a_k the mean of x squared on client k and mu_k its local optimum. We use eta = 0.1, which keeps every client stable since eta times a_k stays below 1.

blocks.prompt: Start from w = 0 and let every client take one local step (E = 1, B = full batch). Client A ends at 0.10, client B at 0.80, client C at 2.70. What does the server set as the new global model?
blocks.reveal:
Not 1.20, which is the plain mean of the three. Weighting by sample count gives

0.5 x 0.10 + (1/3) x 0.80 + (1/6) x 2.70 = 0.050 + 0.267 + 0.450 = **0.766667**

And there is a second, sharper surprise: 0.766667 is exactly what one full-batch gradient step on all 108 pooled points gives. With E = 1 and full participation, FedAvg is not an approximation of centralized gradient descent; it is centralized gradient descent, rearranged.

blocks.title: The weighted average, cell by cell

scenes.caption: Round 1 starts. The server broadcasts w = 0 to all three clients. Sample counts are fixed properties of the clients and are sent back with the update.
Each client takes one local full-batch step toward its own optimum. Client C has the steepest loss (a = 9), so it moves furthest: from 0 to 2.70, nearly all the way to its local optimum of 3.
The server computes the weights. m_t is 108 here because all three clients reported, so the weights are 54/108, 36/108 and 18/108.
Multiply and sum: 0.050 plus 0.267 plus 0.450 is 0.766667. Client C moved ten times further than client A but carries one third of its weight, so the big quiet client dominates.
Round 2 from w = 0.766667. The clients return 0.79, 1.26 and 2.776667, and the weighted average is 1.277778, which again matches a second full-batch gradient step on the pooled data exactly.

blocks.title: Two rounds of FedAvg on three clients

scenes.caption: Round 1, broadcast. Every client starts this round from the same global model, w = 0. That shared starting point is what makes averaging their results sane at all.
Round 1, local training. Each client walks toward its own optimum (1, 2 and 3), at a speed set by its own curvature.
Round 1, aggregation. The weighted average lands at 0.766667, below all but one client, because the largest client wants the smallest slope.
Round 2, broadcast. The clients forget their own round-1 models completely and restart from the server's. Nothing but the global model survives a round boundary.
Round 2, local training. The gaps between clients are smaller now, since they all start closer to their own optima than they did at w = 0.
Round 2, aggregation: 1.277778. Two rounds have covered a bit over half the distance to the optimum of 2.3, and that is with every client reporting every round.

blocks.md: A common misreading is that FedAvg averages the clients' answers. It averages their **parameters**. In this problem the sample-weighted average of the three local optima is 1.667 and the plain average is 2.0, while the true optimum is 2.3. Averaging models that have fully solved their own problems gives the wrong model.

With $E = 1$, full batches and full participation, FedAvg is exactly full-batch gradient descent on the pooled objective. Everything interesting about federated optimization, good and bad, comes from doing more than one local step.

blocks.question: Client A (54 examples) returns 0.10, client B (36) returns 0.80, client C (18) returns 2.70, but this round client B drops out and never reports. What does FedAvg set as the new global model?
options: 0.767, since the weights 54/108, 36/108 and 18/108 are properties of the clients
0.500, the weighted average with client B's contribution set to zero
0.750, the weighted average of A and C renormalized over 72 examples
The round is discarded, because FedAvg requires every selected client
blocks.explain: The denominator is m_t, the examples in this round only: 54 + 18 = 72. So the model is (54/72) x 0.10 + (18/72) x 2.70 = 0.075 + 0.675 = 0.750. Keeping stale weights that sum to less than one (option B) would shrink the model toward zero, and single dropouts never abandon a round.

blocks.question: A client has 800 local examples. You set E = 4 and B = 20. How many SGD updates does it perform per round, and how many parameter vectors does it send?
options: 40 updates, 4 vectors (one per epoch)
160 updates, 1 vector
800 updates, 1 vector
4 updates, 1 vector
blocks.explain: Updates per round are E times n_k divided by B, so 4 x 800 / 20 = 160 steps. All of that local work produces exactly one message: the parameters the client holds when the last epoch ends. That asymmetry between local compute and network traffic is the reason FedAvg exists.

lessons.title: Buying rounds with local work, and when that stops working

blocks.md:
A round costs bytes on a consumer uplink, and it costs minutes of wall-clock time while the server waits. So the metric that matters is rounds to target accuracy, not epochs or examples seen.

Take the convolutional model from the original paper: two 5x5 convolutions, a 512-unit dense layer, 1663370 parameters. At 4 bytes per parameter that is 6.65 MB of model, which every selected client downloads and (roughly) uploads again each round. With $C = 0.1$ over 100 clients, 10 clients participate, so one round moves about 66.5 MB of updates up to the server. The question is how many such rounds you need.

blocks.title: Rounds to 99 percent on MNIST, by how much local work per round

scenes.caption: IID split (data shuffled, 600 examples per client). One gradient step per round needs 626 rounds. Adding local work collapses that to 18 rounds, a 34.8x saving, and it is mostly driven by the smaller batch size.

Pathological non-IID split: data sorted by label, cut into 200 shards of 300, two shards per client, so most clients see only two digits. Every FedAvg setting needs far more rounds, and E=5 with full batches needs 1000, worse than sending single gradients.

blocks.md:
Read the two scenes together. On the IID split the trade is almost free: 626 rounds become 18, so the total upload to reach 99 percent falls from about 41.6 GB to about 1.2 GB (626 x 10 x 6.65 MB against 18 x 10 x 6.65 MB). Meanwhile the local work per client per round goes from 1 SGD update to 1200. You spent device compute, which is idle and free, to buy network rounds, which are scarce.

On the pathological non-IID split the same settings need 173 rounds instead of 18. The saving is real but an order of magnitude smaller, and one setting (E = 5 with full local batches, 1000 rounds) is twice as slow as just sending gradients.

blocks.title: More local work from bigger E or smaller B, same bytes per round

scenes.caption: B = 600 is the whole local dataset: one update per epoch, so u = E. Ten local epochs is ten gradient steps, and the client still uploads one 6.65 MB model.

B = 50 multiplies the updates by 12 at no communication cost at all. The paper's advice is to tune B down first, because lowering it is nearly free as long as B stays large enough to saturate the device's hardware.
B = 10, E = 20: 1200 updates per client per round, against one single update for FedSGD. The upload curve has not moved. That gap is the entire resource argument for FedAvg.

blocks.md:
So why not set $E$ to 1000? Because local work is only useful while the local objectives agree with the global one, and past some point extra local steps move a client toward its own optimum rather than everyone's.

The evidence in the original paper is uneven in an instructive way. On the MNIST convolutional model, large $E$ showed no significant degradation. On a character-level LSTM trained on Shakespeare roles, large numbers of local epochs made FedAvg plateau or diverge. On a large-scale next-word model over more than 500000 authors, $E = 1$ was slightly better than $E = 5$. The paper's suggestion is to decay local computation late in training, the way you decay a learning rate.

blocks.prompt: Your federated run converges steadily at E = 1 and you want it twice as fast, so you set E = 10. Rounds to your accuracy target get worse, not better. What is the most likely cause?
blocks.reveal: The clients disagree. With heterogeneous data, ten local epochs take each client most of the way to its own optimum, and the average of those models is not the model that minimizes the pooled loss. You are converging quickly to the wrong point. The next lesson computes that wrong point exactly on our three-client problem: E = 1 lands on 2.3, E = 5 lands on 1.944, and large E approaches 1.667.

blocks.question: You halve B and keep E fixed. Which quantity changes the most?
options: Bytes uploaded per client per round, which doubles
SGD updates per client per round, which doubles
Rounds to the accuracy target, which always halves
The number of clients the server must wait for
blocks.explain: Updates per round are E times n_k over B, so halving B doubles them. Communication per round is set by the model size, not by B or E: one download and one upload of the parameters. Whether the extra local work converts into fewer rounds depends on how heterogeneous the clients are, so option C is exactly the trap.

blocks.question: In the original experiments, which result shows that more local computation is not always better?
options: On the IID MNIST split, E = 20 with B = 10 needed 18 rounds instead of 626
The model reached a higher final accuracy (99.44 percent) than the gradient-averaging baseline
A client fraction of C = 0.1 worked about as well as C = 1.0
On the non-IID split, E = 5 with full local batches needed 1000 rounds while single gradients needed 483
blocks.explain: That row is the one setting in the table slower than the FedSGD baseline, a 0.5x speedup. It is the fingerprint of local work pulling clients apart. The Shakespeare LSTM shows the same effect more dramatically: with very large E, training can plateau or diverge.

lessons.title: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer

blocks.md:
Non-IID in federated learning is not one phenomenon. The common forms are label skew (one user types in one language, one hospital sees one patient population), quantity skew (one client has 50 examples and another 50000), and feature skew (different sensors, different handwriting). The original paper built the extreme case on purpose: sort MNIST by digit, cut it into 200 shards of 300 examples, and give each of 100 clients 2 shards, so most clients only ever see two digits.

We can get the same effect on our three-client problem by resplitting the same 108 points two ways.

blocks.title: The same 108 points, split two ways

scenes.caption: Skewed split: each client holds exactly one kind of point. Local optima are 1, 2 and 3 and local curvatures are 1, 4 and 9, so the clients disagree about both the answer and how confident they are.
IID split of the identical 108 points: every client gets all three kinds in proportion to its size. Now every client has curvature 10/3 and local optimum 2.3, which is also the global optimum.
Column sums are unchanged (54, 36, 18 points of each kind) and so are the client sizes. Nothing about the data or the objective differs between the two scenes; only who holds what.

blocks.md: Run FedAvg from $w_0 = 0$ with $\eta = 0.1$ on both splits. Because each local problem is a parabola, a client's model after $E$ full-batch steps has a closed form, which makes the whole trajectory exactly computable:

blocks.caption: Each client contracts toward its own optimum by a factor r_k per round. For eta = 0.1 and E = 5: r = 0.590, 0.078, 0.00001 for clients A, B and C. Client C is already sitting on its local optimum when it reports.

blocks.title: IID versus label-skewed, same points, same E

scenes.caption: With E = 1, FedAvg is pooled gradient descent, so the split does not matter at all: both the IID and the skewed run follow this identical curve and reach 2.3 (within 0.01 by round 14).
IID with E = 5: five local steps per round instead of one, and the curve is within 0.01 of the optimum by round 3 instead of round 14. This is the free lunch the previous lesson promised.
Skewed with E = 5: fastest early progress of all three, then it flattens at 1.9439 and stays there forever. It converges, quickly, to a point that is not the optimum. That is client drift.

blocks.md: The flat line is not noise or a bad learning rate. The round map is affine, so it has a fixed point, and we can write it down.

blocks.tex: w_{\infty} = \frac{\sum_k p_k (1 - r_k)\, \mu_k}{\sum_k p_k (1 - r_k)}, \qquad p_k = \frac{n_k}{n}, \quad r_k = (1-\eta a_k)^{E}
blocks.caption: Where FedAvg stops on this problem. For E = 1 this reduces to the true optimum, since 1 minus r_k is exactly eta times a_k and the curvature weighting is restored. For any E above 1 it does not.

blocks.md:
The computed fixed points on the skewed split, all with $\eta = 0.1$:

- $E = 1$: 2.300000, the exact optimum
- $E = 2$: 2.147887
- $E = 5$: 1.943889
- $E = 50$: 1.668389
- $E \to \infty$: 1.666667, which is exactly $\sum_k p_k \mu_k$, the weighted average of the local optima

That limit is the mechanism in one line. As local work grows, each client arrives at its own optimum, so the server averages optima instead of averaging gradients, and the average of the optima is not the optimum of the average. This is the client drift that the SCAFFOLD paper illustrates with exactly this argument: the server update moves toward the mean of the client optima rather than toward the global optimum. On the IID split every $\mu_k$ equals 2.3, so there is nothing to drift to and bigger $E$ is pure profit.

Two well-known corrections, both grounded in the same picture:

**FedProx** adds a proximal term to the local objective, which penalizes moving away from the broadcast model. It also explicitly allows stragglers to send partial work (an inexact local solution) instead of being dropped. The paper reports improving absolute test accuracy by 22 percent on average in highly heterogeneous settings.

**SCAFFOLD** keeps a control variate $c_i$ per client and $c$ on the server, and corrects each local gradient by $c - c_i$ so that local steps point along the global descent direction rather than the local one.

blocks.tex: \min_w h_k(w; w_t) = F_k(w) + \frac{\mu}{2} \lVert w - w_t \rVert^2 \qquad\text{and}\qquad y_i \leftarrow y_i - \eta_l \left( g_i(y_i) + c - c_i \right)
blocks.caption: Left: the FedProx local objective, with mu = 0 recovering FedAvg. Right: one SCAFFOLD local step, where the control variates are initialized to zero and maintained so that c is the mean of the c_i.

blocks.md: On our toy problem, a proximal term with $\mu = 2$ moves the $E = 5$ fixed point from 1.944 to 1.995 and slows the first round from 1.320 to 0.988. It buys accuracy with speed, and it does not reach 2.3. Treat these methods as damping on drift, not as a cure; the honest cure for this toy is $E = 1$ or a control-variate correction.

Simplified model: ours is one parameter, convex, deterministic, full-batch and fully participating. Real drift in a deep network is worse and messier (it interacts with batch normalization statistics, momentum and client sampling), but the direction of the error is the one computed here.

blocks.question: On the skewed split with E = 5, FedAvg flattens out at 1.944 while the optimum is 2.3. What is the single most reliable fix if you must keep that exact data split?
options: Raise the client fraction C so more clients report each round
Train for ten times as many rounds at E = 5
Do less local work per round (smaller E) or correct the local gradients, which both reduce drift
Increase the local learning rate so clients get closer to their local optima
blocks.explain: 1.944 is a fixed point, so more rounds change nothing, and all three clients already report every round so C is irrelevant here. Getting closer to the local optima makes the drift worse: that is the E tending to infinity limit of 1.667. Reducing local work or correcting the local direction (FedProx, SCAFFOLD) attacks the actual cause.

blocks.question: A colleague says FedAvg with E = 5 was fine on their IID benchmark, so the non-IID result must be a bug. What is the right response?
options: They are right: FedAvg is split-independent by construction
With IID clients every local optimum equals the global one, so there is nothing to drift toward; the skew is what creates the bias
The IID result must also be biased, just less visibly
Drift only appears when clients have different sample counts
blocks.explain: In our IID split every client has curvature 10/3 and local optimum 2.3, so the fixed point is 2.3 for any E and larger E is pure speedup. Unequal sample counts alone are harmless, since FedAvg already weights by n_k; what hurts is local objectives that disagree with the pooled one.

lessons.title: Stragglers, partial participation and the round quorum

blocks.md:
In a production cross-device system a client is eligible only when it is idle, charging and on an unmetered network such as wifi. Tens of thousands of devices may announce availability in a window, and the server invites typically a few hundred of them to a round.

A round then has three phases. **Selection**: eligible devices check in on a bidirectional stream and the server picks a subset; the phase ends when a participant goal count is reached or a timeout fires. **Configuration**: the server sends the training plan and the current model. **Reporting**: the server waits for updates, aggregates them as they arrive, and closes the round if enough devices reported in time. If not enough did, the round is abandoned and nothing is applied.

blocks.title: One round: the server closes on a quorum, not on everyone

scenes.caption: Selection. Eligible devices check in; the server accepts until it has its goal count or the selection timeout fires. Devices it does not want are told when to come back.
Configuration. Each participant downloads the plan and the global model. Download traffic dominates upload, because the plan is comparable in size to the model and updates compress better.
Local training, and devices are not alike. Device 4 is slow: older hardware, more local examples, or a user who picked the phone up. The server simply waits with a deadline.
Reporting. Updates arrive and are aggregated online as they come in, so the server never has to store them all. Three of four have reported by t = 135 seconds.
The quorum is met, the round closes, and device 4's upload at t = 175 is rejected: it arrives after the reporting window. In one measured population 22 percent of sessions ended exactly this way.

blocks.md:
The operational numbers from a production deployment make the design concrete.

- Between 6 and 10 percent of selected devices drop out per round (computation errors, network failures, or losing eligibility because the user picked up the phone), so the server selects about **130 percent** of the target count. Target 100, invite 130, expect 117 to 122 alive, close the round at 100 and abort the extra.
- Of on-device training sessions: 75 percent completed and were accepted, 22 percent completed but were rejected because they reported after the window closed, 2 percent were interrupted before finishing.
- The system handled roughly 10 million daily active devices with up to 10000 participating simultaneously, and a 4x difference between daytime and nighttime participation for a US-centric population.
- For the next-word model, a round took two to three minutes and 3000 rounds took 5 days.

Partial participation interacts badly with skew, which you can see on our three-client problem. Suppose the server samples one client per round instead of all three, round robin, with $E = 5$. The weighting does nothing now, because the only reporting client gets weight $n_k/m_t = 1$, so the global model is dragged to whichever client happened to be picked.

blocks.title: Global model after each round: all clients versus one per round

scenes.caption: All three clients every round, E = 5. Monotone and boring: it settles on its (biased) fixed point 1.9439 within four rounds and stays there.
One client per round, cycling A, C, B. The model is yanked to 3.0 whenever client C is picked and back down when A is. With E = 5 the server is effectively adopting one client's local answer.

blocks.md:
Real systems avoid that oscillation by sampling hundreds of clients per round, so the round's data distribution is close to the population's, and by keeping the client fraction modest ($C = 0.1$ in the original experiments; a few hundred devices per round was found sufficient in production, with diminishing returns beyond that). It is averaging over clients within a round, not across rounds, that stabilizes the update.

The server also paces check-ins. A flow-control mechanism tells rejected devices when to reconnect, which both avoids a thundering herd for large populations and gathers enough simultaneous devices for small ones.

A federated round is a **rendezvous with a quorum**, not a barrier over all clients. The server waits for a minimum percentage of a goal count within a time window, aggregates whoever made it, ignores the stragglers, and abandons the round if too few arrive.

blocks.question: You need 200 reporting devices per round and measure an 8 percent dropout rate. How many should you invite, and what happens to the extras?
options: Exactly 200, and retry the ones that fail inside the same round
About 260 (130 percent), closing the round once 200 have reported and aborting the rest
As many as check in, aggregating every update that ever arrives
400, so that a full round survives even if half the devices vanish
blocks.explain: Over-selecting by about 130 percent is the deployed practice: it absorbs the 6 to 10 percent that drop out and lets the slowest tail be discarded. The round closes on the quorum, and the surplus tail gets aborted, which is why 22 percent of sessions in the measured population finished training but had their result rejected.

blocks.question: Why does sampling only one client per round make the oscillation above so violent, while sampling 300 clients per round does not?
options: A single client's update is noisier, but the drift direction is unaffected
FedAvg cannot weight a single client correctly
The oscillation is a learning-rate artifact that more clients happen to damp
With one client the round's data distribution is that client's distribution, while 300 clients approximate the population
blocks.explain: The weighted average is a sample estimate of the population objective. With one skewed client per round, the server is optimizing that client's objective for a whole round; with hundreds, the mixture is close to the population and the averaging inside the round smooths the local optima together. FedAvg does weight one client correctly: the weight is 1.

lessons.title: What the server sees: secure aggregation, DP, and Flower

blocks.md:
Keeping raw data on the device is not the same as keeping it private. A plain FedAvg server receives one parameter vector per client per round, and a model update computed from a few hundred examples carries information about those examples; for a language model it can carry rare strings nearly verbatim.

Two defenses attack two different problems. **Secure aggregation** stops the server from seeing any individual update while still letting it compute the sum. **Differential privacy** limits what the aggregate itself reveals about any one contributor. They compose, and neither replaces the other.

Secure aggregation is built from pairwise masks. Every pair of users agrees on two random vectors and forms $p_{u,v} = s_{u,v} - s_{v,u} \bmod R$, which has the property $p_{u,v} = -p_{v,u}$. Each user adds all its pairwise masks to its own value and uploads the result. Individually those uploads look uniformly random; summed, every mask cancels against its partner.

blocks.tex: y_u = x_u + b_u + \sum_{v} p_{u,v} \bmod R, \qquad p_{u,v} = -p_{v,u} \;\Longrightarrow\; \sum_u y_u = \sum_u x_u \bmod R
blocks.caption: The masking identity, with b_u an extra per-user mask explained below. Updates are mapped into integers mod R by clipping, scaling and quantizing them first.

blocks.title: Three users, one scalar each, mod 100

scenes.caption: Each pair exchanges two random seeds over an authenticated channel (relayed by the server but encrypted end to end). A and B derive p_AB = 47 and p_BA = 53, which sum to 100, that is 0 mod 100.

The private values are 12, 30 and 55. Masks are 11, 97 and 92, so the uploads are 23, 27 and 47. Not one of those three numbers is close to the value it hides, and the server cannot tell them from random.
The true sum is 12 + 30 + 55 = 97. The server learned the sum and nothing else: no individual value, and no way to subtract one user out. Simplified: this figure uses the pairwise masks only.

Now user C drops out before uploading. Its masks no longer cancel, so the sum is garbage. Recovery: each user also secret-shared its seeds, so the server can ask the survivors to reconstruct C's masks.

blocks.md:
Dropout recovery is where the protocol earns the word practical. Each user splits its secrets with a $(t, n)$ threshold scheme (Shamir sharing) with $t > n/2$, so any $t$ survivors can reconstruct a dropped user's masks and the sum still comes out.

That alone would break privacy: a server could falsely declare a live user dropped and ask for its masks. Hence the second, individual mask $b_u$. In the unmasking round the server must choose, per user, either the shares of that user's pairwise seeds (if it claims the user dropped) or the shares of $b_u$ (if the user survived), and an honest survivor never gives both. So every value stays hidden behind one mask or the other. The protocol tolerates up to one third of users failing to complete it, and costs about 1.73x the bytes of sending data in the clear for 16-bit input values, $2^{10}$ users and $2^{20}$-dimensional vectors.

Secure aggregation hides *who contributed what*. It does not make the result safe to publish: the sum of 100 updates can still reveal a rare phrase typed by one user. For that you need noise, and a budget that accounts for every round you release.

Differentially private federated averaging makes four changes to FedAvg: select users by independent sampling with probability $q$ rather than taking a fixed count, clip each user's update so its L2 norm is at most $S$ (flat, or per layer), form the bounded-sensitivity weighted average, and add Gaussian noise to that average. The result is reported as an $(\epsilon, \delta)$ guarantee: $\epsilon$ bounds how much the distribution over released models can shift when one user is added or removed, so a smaller $\epsilon$ is a stronger promise, and $\delta$ is the small probability that the bound fails. Privacy loss across rounds is tracked with the moments accountant, the bookkeeping from the DP-SGD line of work that composes those per-round bounds into one $\epsilon$. The unit of protection is the **user**, not the example: the guarantee is about datasets that differ by one user's entire contribution.

blocks.caption: Clip, then average, then noise. Simplified: the paper defines the sensitivity S-tilde of the exact weighted-average estimator and sets the noise relative to it, and the accountant needs the random user sampling to get amplification.

blocks.title: Privacy budget after 5000 rounds of the same LSTM

scenes.caption: Epsilon on a dataset of 763430 users, at delta = 1e-9, with 5000, 1667 and 1250 users expected per round. More noise buys a smaller epsilon. The no-noise run has no guarantee at all (epsilon unbounded), so its bar is drawn at zero.
The same three configurations on a population of 1e8 users: epsilon 1.152, 0.991 and 0.987. Nothing about the noise changed. Privacy got cheaper purely because each user is one of far more.

blocks.md:
And the utility cost, measured as top-1 next-word accuracy after 5000 rounds on the 763430-user dataset: 17.62 percent with no noise, 17.49 percent at epsilon 4.63, 17.04 percent at epsilon 2.31, 16.33 percent at epsilon 2.04.

So the tradeoff is not mainly accuracy, it is compute. The non-private baseline reached 17.5 percent using 100 users per round; matching that accuracy with a (4.6, 1e-9) guarantee needed about 5000 users per round, roughly 60x more work, because larger noise has to be averaged over more contributions. The paper's summary is that with enough users, privacy costs computation rather than utility.

Finally, what a framework gives you. Flower splits a federated system into a **ServerApp** holding a *strategy* (who is selected, how updates are combined) and a **ClientApp** holding local training. Named strategies ship with it, including FedAvg, FedProx, FedAdam, FedAvgM and FedMedian, so the choices from this course are constructor arguments rather than code.

Its simulation runtime (built on Ray) runs many virtual clients, called SuperNodes, on one machine: you set how many with a federation config and how much CPU or GPU each ClientApp gets, and the maximum parallelism is whichever of those limits binds first. The ClientApp objects are the same ones the deployment runtime uses, where a long-lived SuperLink coordinates SuperNodes on real devices. The Flower paper reports experiments up to 15 million clients in client-population size using a pair of high-end GPUs.

blocks.code:
# ServerApp side: the strategy is where C, the weighting and the quorum live
from flwr.serverapp.strategy import FedAvg

strategy = FedAvg(
    fraction_train=0.1,              # C: sample 10 percent of connected nodes
    min_train_nodes=10,              # never run a round with fewer than 10
    min_available_nodes=100,         # wait until 100 nodes are connected
    weighted_by_key="num-examples",  # the n_k that FedAvg weights by
)

# ClientApp side: identical code in simulation and in deployment
app = ClientApp()

@app.train()
def train(msg: Message, context: Context):
    model.load_state_dict(msg.content["arrays"].to_torch_state_dict())
    loss = train_fn(model, trainloader, epochs=1)   # E local epochs
    metrics = {"train_loss": loss,
               "num-examples": len(trainloader.dataset)}
    content = RecordDict({"arrays": ArrayRecord(model.state_dict()),
                          "metrics": MetricRecord(metrics)})
    return Message(content=content, reply_to=msg)
blocks.caption: Shape taken from the Flower docs: the FedAvg strategy reference (its defaults are fraction_train 1.0, min_train_nodes 2, weighted_by_key num-examples) and the PyTorch quickstart. The client returns parameters plus the n_k the server weights by.

blocks.md: The one thing to remember: federated learning is an optimization algorithm shaped by a systems constraint. Every piece (averaging instead of gradient sharing, a quorum instead of a barrier, masks instead of raw updates, noise instead of trust) exists because rounds are expensive, clients are unreliable, and the server is not allowed to look.

blocks.question: Under secure aggregation with 500 clients in a round, what does an honest-but-curious server learn?
options: Each client's update, but only in encrypted form it cannot use
The sum of the 500 masked updates, from which it can subtract any client it chooses
Nothing at all, including the sum, until a trusted third party decrypts it
The sum of the 500 updates and nothing about any individual update
blocks.explain: The functionality is exactly summation: the server learns the sum and no individual contribution. It cannot subtract one client out, because each client's value is covered by masks that only cancel in the full sum, and the per-user mask b_u blocks the attack of falsely declaring a live client dropped.

blocks.question: Your DP federated run has far worse accuracy than the non-private baseline at the same epsilon. Which change most directly fixes it, according to the published results?
options: Sample many more users per round, so the same noise is averaged over more clipped updates
Lower the clipping norm S, so each update contributes less
Reduce the number of rounds, since every round spends privacy budget
Switch from user-level to example-level accounting and report that instead
blocks.explain: Noise is added once per round to the average, so more users per round shrinks its relative size at fixed epsilon: matching the baseline needed about 5000 users per round instead of 100, roughly 60x the compute. Lowering S adds clipping bias, and with large populations extra rounds cost very little budget (epsilon moved from 0.84 to 0.88 over a million rounds at 1e9 users).

blocks.question: You want to try FedProx instead of FedAvg in a Flower project. What has to change?
options: The ClientApp, since the proximal term is a local objective
Both apps, plus the simulation runtime configuration
Only the strategy object in the ServerApp, which is what selects clients and aggregates
Nothing: Flower chooses an aggregation rule automatically from the data
blocks.explain: Flower ships FedProx alongside FedAvg, FedAdam, FedAvgM and FedMedian as strategies, so swapping the algorithm is a ServerApp change. Note the honest caveat: a strategy can set the proximal coefficient for clients to use, but the proximal penalty itself is computed during local training, so a real FedProx run also needs the client loss to include it.
